Main problems this produces
- Big error code dominates but provides no action: a very large “404” draws attention but doesn’t help the user recover. It creates emphasis without directing behavior.
- Small explanatory text is too weak to guide users: apology copy that’s too small is easily missed and provides little context or reassurance.

1. Make the recovery action immediate and prominent
   - Why: Users come to a 404 to recover quickly. Primary actions should be obvious and above the fold.
   - How: Move the search box and primary CTA closer to the center under the explanatory message. Give the primary CTA (e.g., "Back to home" or "Take me home") higher visual weight — solid color, larger size, clear contrast, and a primary placement to the right of or above the search on desktop; stack vertically on mobile.

2. Rebalance the hierarchy between code and message
   - Why: The error code is useful for debugging but shouldn’t be the strongest call-to-action.
   - How: Reduce the 404 size or tone it down (lighter weight or lower contrast) and increase the size / prominence of the explanatory headline and action area. Make a short clear headline (e.g., “Page not found”) larger than the apology line so users immediately know the problem and next steps.

3. Strengthen the explanatory copy and add a quick path
   - Why: Small apology copy is often not helpful. Users need context and a next step.
   - How: Replace or supplement the tiny apology line with a concise sentence and an explicit recovery hint (e.g., “We can’t find that page. Try searching or return to the homepage.”). Add one helpful link (popular pages or “Contact support”) near the CTA/search.

4. Make search the obvious recovery tool
   - Why: Search is often the quickest way for a user to find what they wanted.
   - How: Make the search field visually prominent: wider, higher-contrast border or filled background, placeholder text that suggests examples (“Search for articles, product names…”). Ensure it receives focus by default if appropriate (consider accessibility/annoyance tradeoffs).

5. Improve contrast and accessibility
   - Why: Grey low-contrast elements and small typography hurt readability.
   - How: Ensure text and controls meet contrast ratios (WCAG) — especially button labels and the apology/explanatory text. Use readable font sizes and adequate line-height. Make touch targets at least 44px high on mobile; ensure logical focus order and ARIA labels for search and button.

6. Provide helpful links and context, but don’t clutter
   - Why: Footer links are useful, but when they’re visually similar and tucked away they aren’t helpful.
   - How: Offer 3–5 suggested links (home, most popular sections, contact) near the main action area rather than only in the footer. Keep footer links, but visually separate them as secondary.

7. Improve tone and microcopy
   - Why: 404s can be frustrating — tone can reduce friction.
   - How: Use brief, friendly copy. If appropriate for your brand, a small illustration or humanizing line can reassure users — but keep it optional and subtle.

8. Mobile responsiveness and stacking
   - Why: Layout that works on desktop may bury actions on small screens.
   - How: On narrow viewports stack elements vertically in this order: (logo/header) → concise headline → explanatory text → search → primary CTA → secondary links → footer. Ensure the search and CTA remain above the fold on typical phone screen sizes.

- [ ] Move search and primary CTA up and make them visually prominent.
- [ ] Ensure color contrast and readable font sizes (WCAG AA/AAA where feasible).
- [ ] Add one or two helpful links (popular pages/contact) near actions.
- [ ] Ensure keyboard focus order and ARIA labels for search/button.
- [ ] Test on mobile to confirm search/CTA are above the fold and touch targets are large enough.

Short answer
- A “searchable” PDF contains actual text characters the PDF viewer can find, select, copy, and index.
- A “scanned” (image-only) PDF contains page images (bitmaps) of the paper; there’s no text layer so you can’t search/select/copy until OCR is run.

What’s different inside the file
- Content layer
  - Searchable (born-digital or OCR’ed): pages include text objects (glyphs with font info and character codes) placed at positions on the page.
  - Scanned/image-only: pages are just images (JPEG/PNG/CCITT etc.) with no underlying text objects.
- How search works
  - If text objects exist, the viewer’s Find/Index features match those characters.
  - If only images exist, Find can’t match anything unless OCR added a text layer.
- OCR vs original text
  - OCR can add an invisible text layer aligned to the image (you see the picture, but the PDF also contains selectable text). Searchable doesn’t guarantee perfect text—OCR errors can produce wrong characters.
- Accessibility/structure
  - Searchable text ≠ accessible. For screen readers you also want a tagged/structured PDF (logical reading order and tags). A searchable PDF may have text but no tags.
- File size & composition
  - Scanned images can make large files unless compressed. Born-digital/searchable PDFs often have smaller sizes because text and vectors are compact; they may also embed fonts.

Quick ways to tell (demonstrations for your coworker)
- Try to select some text or use Find. If it works, the PDF has text.
- Save/export to plain text (or “Save as Text”)—if it returns readable text it’s searchable.
- In Adobe Reader: File → Properties → Fonts shows embedded fonts if it’s text-based.
- Command line: tools like pdffonts (poppler) list fonts; if none, it’s probably image-only.

One more note
- You can have a hybrid: image visible + invisible OCR text layer (common for scanned-then-OCR PDFs). It looks like a scan but is searchable.

Elevator pitch
- A "scanned PDF" is basically a picture of each page (so you can’t search, select, or copy the words). A "searchable PDF" contains real text data (either because it was created from a digital text source or because OCR added a hidden text layer) so you can search, select, and extract the text.

What’s actually different inside the file
- Scanned (image-only) PDF
  - Each page is stored as an image (JPEG, TIFF, etc.) embedded in the PDF.
  - No text objects exist for the words on the page — the PDF only contains pixels.
  - Result: you cannot search for words, select or copy text, or reliably extract text programmatically.

- Born-digital PDF (true text PDF)
  - The file contains real text objects (PDF text operators and font resources).
  - Fonts may be embedded; text is selectable, searchable, and exact (no OCR errors).
  - Created from digital sources (Word, InDesign, web, print-to-PDF).

- Searchable PDF from a scan (often called a “sandwich PDF”)
  - The original page image is embedded for visual fidelity, AND an invisible text layer produced by OCR is added on top of (or under) the image.
  - Visually it looks like the scan, but the invisible text layer makes the document searchable/selectable.
  - OCR can introduce recognition errors and wrong character positions, so copy/paste may not always be perfect.

Other related differences
- Accessibility tags: an “accessible PDF” has structural tags/reading order for screen readers (this is separate from merely being searchable).
- File size: image-only scanned PDFs can be large; adding an OCR text layer adds little size but OCRed images may get re-compressed.
- Privacy: a searchable/scanned+OCR PDF exposes the document’s text even if you only see an image, so redaction must target the text layer too.

Quick ways to tell the difference
- Try to select text with the mouse. If you can highlight and copy words, it has selectable text.
- Search for a known word (Ctrl+F). If it finds it, there’s text data.
- Try copying and pasting some text to a text editor — OCR errors are visible in sandwich PDFs.
- In Adobe Acrobat: Properties → Fonts will list embedded fonts for true text PDFs. Accessibility or “Read Out Loud” may indicate text presence.
- Command-line: run pdftotext file.pdf (or pdfinfo) — if pdftotext extracts readable content, it’s not image-only.
- Open the PDF in a plain text editor and search for an obvious word — if you find readable fragments, it likely contains text objects (not guaranteed because some PDFs compress/encode text).

Tips for explaining to your coworker
- Use an analogy: “Scanned = photograph of a page. Searchable = photograph plus an invisible transcript glued to it, or else a digital document where the words are stored directly.”
- Add a demo: open a scan, try Ctrl+F and selecting text — that quickly shows the difference.

Caveat
- Searchable ≠ perfect. OCR introduces mistakes (especially with unusual fonts, poor scan quality, or columns), and “searchable” doesn’t imply the document is accessible (proper tags for screen readers may still be missing).

Good question — converting a formula-heavy sheet to CSV can silently change or break things. Short checklist plus step-by-step to reduce risk:

Quick checklist (what to watch for)
- Formulas will be lost in a CSV. Any SUMIFs or other formulas must be converted to plain values if the portal expects numbers.
- References to other sheets will break if the other sheet isn’t included; the CSV contains only that single sheet.
- Hidden rows/columns, filters, pivot tables, data validation, conditional formatting, and comments are not preserved in CSV.
- Number formatting (currency symbols, thousands separators, parentheses for negatives), date formats, and percent displays may be interpreted differently by the portal — check raw values and formats.
- Locale issues: decimal separator (dot vs comma) and CSV delimiter (comma vs semicolon).
- Encoding: portals often require UTF‑8 (or sometimes Windows-1252). Also check whether a BOM is needed.
- Text fields containing commas, quotes or newlines must be properly quoted; some exports handle this automatically, some portals mis-handle it.
- Leading zeros (IDs) can be lost if treated as numeric instead of text.
- Rounding/precision: SUMIFs may produce long decimals — round if portal expects fixed decimals.
- Error cells (#REF!, #N/A, #DIV/0!) export as text and may cause portal rejects.
- Column order and headers must match the finance portal’s template.

Step-by-step safe workflow
1. Make a backup copy of the workbook (preserve formulas).
2. Confirm portal requirements: required columns, column order, delimiter, encoding, date format, required precision/decimals, and whether negative numbers/currency are allowed.
3. In a copy workbook, create a snapshot sheet:
   - Option A: Duplicate the tab, then select all and Paste Special → Values (Excel/Sheets) to replace formulas with their current values.
   - Option B: If only some ranges use external refs, select those ranges and Paste Special → Values.
4. Resolve external references:
   - If SUMIFs depend on another sheet, either:
     - Consolidate the referenced data into the same workbook/tab before taking the snapshot, or
     - Ensure you paste values so the totals don’t depend on the other sheet.
   - Watch for INDIRECT/REF formulas — they may produce stale or error values when moved.
5. Check and fix data types:
   - Ensure ID columns with leading zeros are text (prepend apostrophe or format as text).
   - Remove currency symbols if portal expects a numeric field (or confirm portal accepts them).
   - Convert percentages to the numeric form expected (0.12 vs 12%).
6. Check for errors and unusual values:
   - Find/replace or manually fix cells with #REF!, #N/A, #DIV/0!, or blanks where a value is required.
7. Normalize formats:
   - Use ISO date format (YYYY-MM-DD) unless portal requests otherwise.
   - Round to the required number of decimal places.
   - Remove thousands separators from numeric fields (export tools usually do this).
8. Remove hidden content:
   - Unhide rows/columns and verify nothing sensitive or accidental is included.
   - Remove or review notes, comments, or extra metadata you do not want exported.
9. Final verification:
   - Recalculate totals in the snapshot and compare with the original totals to ensure values match.
   - Do a visual scan for odd text like embedded commas/newlines in free-text fields that could break the CSV.
10. Export:
   - Excel: Save As → CSV UTF-8 (Comma delimited) if portal accepts UTF‑8, or the CSV type specified by the portal.

   - Alternatively, export with the delimiter/encoding required by the portal.
11. Test upload:

- Keep a “values-only” copy and a log of changes (what you pasted as values, rounding applied).
